key_features.classic_presentation: ONSET: GRADUAL onset 6-8 weeks after last menstrual period. Initially mild, becomes SUDDEN SEVERE if rupture. LOCATION: UNILATERAL LOWER ABDOMINAL/PELVIC PAIN. Adnexal region (one side). Shoulder pain if ruptured (hemoperitoneum). DURATION: Initially intermittent cramping over days. Becomes CONSTANT if rupture occurs. Pain progresses over hours to days. CHARACTER: Initially CRAMPY, becomes SHARP and SEVERE if rupture. Stabbing pain with rupture. AGGRAVATING: MOVEMENT may worsen. Physical activity can precipitate rupture. Jarring intensifies if ruptured. RELIEVING: NOTHING relieves effectively. Position doesn't help significantly. Requires surgical intervention (salpingectomy/salpingostomy). TIMING: Initially INTERMITTENT cramping. Becomes CONSTANT and severe with rupture. Progressive worsening. SEVERITY: 4-7/10 initially, 9-10/10 if ruptured. Catastrophic with rupture. ASSOCIATED SYMPTOMS: MISSED PERIOD, vaginal spotting (lighter than period), dizziness, lightheadedness. If ruptured: syncope, peritoneal signs. PREGNANCY TEST POSITIVE. KEY POSITIVES: Positive pregnancy test + unilateral pelvic pain + vaginal bleeding. Prior ectopic, pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), IUD use. KEY NEGATIVES: NEGATIVE pregnancy test essentially rules out.

red_flags: LIFE-THREATENING if ruptured - sudden severe pain with hypotension/syncope - call 911
Shoulder pain with abdominal pain in pregnant woman - ruptured ectopic with hemoperitoneum
Positive pregnancy test + abdominal pain - ALWAYS get ultrasound to rule out ectopic
ANY female of childbearing age with abdominal pain needs pregnancy test
